newsitem.title: UK: UK retail spree unlikely after lacklustre Xmas.
newsitem.headline: UK retail spree unlikely after lacklustre Xmas.

text.p: British consumers, who watched their pennies over Christmas, are unlikely to give store owners a runaway sales boom in 1997, but a housing upturn and cash windfalls could still make it a good year.
Investors are nervous after very mixed reports on Christmas from British retailers, which included some nasty shocks, industry analysts said Wednesday.
But they predicted 1997 could still stand out as one of the better years for retail sales, with big ticket consumer durables and electricals selling well.

"We are quite optimistic that 1997 will turn out to be one of the best years of the 1990s," said Richard Hyman, chairman of retail analyst Verdict, which is forecasting a 5.9 percent increase in sales for the year.
Other industry watchers agreed that last year's upturn would carry on into 1997, with consumer confidence bolstered by the revival of the housing market.

But the surprise sales slowdown in December, when retail sales fell versus November, showed shoppers remembered the lessons of the 1980s and were not going for a credit-fuelled spending spree, they said.
"The consumer environment will be relatively robust, but sales may not keep up the pace seen in 1996," said another retail analyst, who asked to remain anonymous.
Retail sector leader Marks and Spencer Plc, one of the last retailers to report on Christmas, disappointed investors with its sales performance, and its shares fell after rising steeply on Tuesday.
"They've clearly done all right overall," said one sector analyst, "but they were a bit weaker over Christmas than some people had hoped."
Sales in the five weeks to January 4 were 6.8 percent overall, with clothing up 7.2 percent, homeware up 27.7 percent and foods 4.9 percent.
Rival clothing retailer Next said earlier in January it had achieved a 14 percent increase in sales in the 24 weeks to January 11, on selling space which was five percent higher.

Bookseller and news distribution firm W.H. Smith Group Plc, battling to recover from a loss last year, produced an encouraging three percent gain in sales over Christmas. And first half profits more than doubled to 38.6 million pounds ($62.5 million).

Analysts said retailers' Christmas trading statements proved shoppers' were still looking for value-for-money. They predicted consumers' thrifty approach, plus intense competition for sales would keep retailers on their toes and make price increases very difficult achieve.

Demand was unlikely to be strong enough to cover up the weaknesses of some firms. Hyman at Verdict predicted it would be a critical year for W.H. Smith Group Plc, Sears Plc, House of Fraser Plc and Etam Plc.
But some of the cash from building society flotations this year -- expected to pump between 18 to 20 billion pounds into the economy -- would end up in retailers' pockets.
"Some of it may have already been spent, some will probably be rolled over into other savings, but there will be a temptation to spend at least some of it," said another retail analyst.

The success stories are likely to remain well-run firms with strong brands -- such as Next and Marks and Spencer Plc -- as well as those benefiting from increased housing related spending such as Kingfisher Plc which owns home decor firm B&Q. And the boom in personal computers is expected to continue to drive profits forward at Dixons Group Plc.
